verses.note: The one who crushes the serpent is himself wounded. The New Testament presents Christ's death as the defeat of the devil (Hebrews 2:14, Colossians 2:15), a victory won through being struck.

Noah comes before God on the far side of judgment by way of a sacrifice. The verse does not say what the offering accomplished, but in Israel's law the burnt offering was accepted “to make atonement” for the worshiper (Leviticus 1:4), and the new world's first act of worship takes that shape.

The promise follows directly on the LORD's smelling “the pleasing aroma” of the sacrifice. The verse ties God's decision to bear with the world to an accepted offering, a connection the New Testament uses when it calls Christ's death a fragrant offering to God (Ephesians 5:2).

Isaac's question, where is the lamb, is the question the whole sacrificial system will keep asking. Abraham's answer, that God will provide it, is taken up by John the Baptist when he names Jesus "the Lamb of God" (John 1:29).

The narrator describes Isaac with the vocabulary of an animal sacrifice. The reader is made to feel what a sacrificial death means when the victim is a beloved son. Isaiah 53:7 pictures the servant of the LORD led like a lamb to the slaughter, silent as Isaac is here.

The ram dies instead of Isaac. The principle of substitution, one life given in place of another, is stated here in its simplest form. The New Testament describes Christ's death with the same logic, the righteous for the unrighteous (1 Peter 3:18) and a ransom for many (Mark 10:45).

The verse uses the vocabulary of atonement in its everyday sense: turning away a wronged party's anger by a costly gift. Israel's sacrifices would later use the same word, with the difference that God himself provides the means by which his face is turned toward his people (Leviticus 17:11).

The chapter never calls Jacob's gift a sacrifice, but it borrows the words for one: covering the face, the offering, the acceptance. Between people, as between God and people, the Old Testament knows that a wrong needs more than time to be put right. The chapter's grace, though, runs the other way: Esau's welcome comes before the gift is accepted.

Judah does not offer a substitute victim, as Reuben offered his sons (42:37). He puts himself under the liability. The verse is not a prophecy, but it is the first clear step toward the substitution of 44:33, where he asks to bear the penalty in Benjamin's place.

Judah offers his own freedom so that Benjamin may go free. This is substitution in the plainest sense, one taking another's place under a penalty, and Genesis uses the same preposition for the ram offered in Isaac's place (22:13). The New Testament does not cite this verse, but the pattern it shows is the one the gospel fulfills.

Blood stands between Moses' family and death, and the scene comes just before the Passover, where the blood on the doorposts will protect Israel's firstborn from the destroyer (12:13). Many interpreters see the night on the road as a small anticipation of that night.

The lamb that stands between the household and death has to be without defect. The same demand governs every sacrifice in Leviticus, and the New Testament applies it to Christ, who offered himself unblemished to God (Hebrews 9:14) and redeemed his people with blood like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Peter 1:19).

The blood stands between the household and the plague. Whether the Passover is classed with the atoning sacrifices or apart from them, the verse establishes that a life given in the house's place is what turns judgment away, the logic Leviticus 17:11 later states for all sacrificial blood.
The answer the children are given calls the rite a sacrifice. The Passover lamb is not merely food but a victim slain to the LORD, and the protection of the household is bound to its death.

The firstborn son is redeemed by a substitute. The law keeps alive the memory of the Passover night, when Israel's firstborn were spared (13:14-15), and establishes that a life claimed by God may be ransomed by a price he accepts.

Even the one who mediates atonement needs it. The priest's own sin offering comes first, a feature Hebrews singles out when it contrasts Aaron with a high priest who had no need to offer for himself (Hebrews 7:27).
The people's sin is dealt with by the same means as the priest's: blood brought before God. No one enters with the blood but the high priest, but the benefit belongs to the whole assembly (verse 17).

The day's work is double. The blood rite cleanses God's house; the live goat removes the people's guilt. Both are needed for God to go on dwelling among them, and the verse marks the hinge between them.

Sin is transferred and removed. The live goat is not killed; it carries guilt away where it can no longer touch the people. Psalm 103:12 and Micah 7:19 use similar pictures of distance and removal for God's forgiveness.

The goat bears the guilt of others. Isaiah 53 uses the same verb of the servant who bore the sin of many (Isaiah 53:12), and although the New Testament does not quote this chapter's goat directly, the language of one who carries away sin runs through its presentation of Christ (John 1:29; 1 Peter 2:24).

The day's result is cleansing ‘from all your sins’. Leviticus presents it as a real and complete provision for Israel's life with God in its time; Hebrews 10:1-4 and 10:11-14 argue that its yearly repetition showed it pointed beyond itself to a sacrifice that would need no repeating.

The day's power lay in God's appointment and in its annual return. Hebrews contrasts ‘once a year’ with ‘once for all’: the yearly rite recalled sins every year (Hebrews 10:3), while Christ appeared ‘once for all at the end of the ages to do away with sin by the sacrifice of Himself’ (Hebrews 9:26).

The verse explains why blood atones rather than simply asserting that it does: blood is life, and God has appointed life given up on the altar to cover the worshipers' lives. Whether that is best described as substitution, ransom, purification, or identification is debated among Christian and Jewish readers, but all agree the means of atonement is God's gift.
The prohibition protects the meaning of the altar. What God has set apart as the means of atonement cannot also be ordinary food, just as holy things in Leviticus cannot be used for common purposes.

Christians have long disagreed about what Jesus' use of this line means. Some stress that citing a psalm's opening evoked the whole psalm, including its vindication; others, including Luther and Calvin, held that Christ truly bore God's judgment on sin and experienced abandonment in his human soul; Jürgen Moltmann (The Crucified God, 1972) read the cry as God's own entry into godforsakenness. Classical theology adds that the Son's cry does not divide the Trinity; it is the true cry of his human nature bearing sin.

Whichever reading is right, the verse pictures the sufferer's hands and feet exposed to his attackers. Christian readers have seen in it the shape of the crucifixion, but the church's reading of Psalm 22 as a passion psalm rests on the Gospels' use of verses 1, 7-8, and 18, not on this verse alone.

The Gospels saw in this verse the literal dispossession of Jesus at his execution. The one who was stripped of everything is, in the psalm's movement, the one whose rescue brings the nations to worship.
